title: Staggered health gating and tokenized readiness windows to stabilize autoscaling during cross-region flapping
creator: Aisha Kumar
description: Background: During the last simulated regional outage test we observed rapid toggle behavior: endpoints in the failover region flip readiness/liveness rapidly when upstream storage or KV cache transiently degrades, causing the autoscaler to overscale then quickly downscale. This creates noisy replicas, cold caches, and repeated request throttling that violates our P99 latency SLO and increases cost. Goal: Introduce a coordinated, instance-level ‘health gating’ mechanism with tokenized readiness windows and staggered readiness release so autoscaler decisions reflect stabilized health signals rather than transient flapping. We aim to reduce autoscaler churn, keep steady serving capacity in failover events, and preserve latency SLOs while limiting cost blowouts.
acceptance_criteria: Autoscaler churn (scale-up/scale-down cycles) observed during a 30m cross-region failover simulation reduced by >= 60% compared to baseline
P99 RL latency across affected services remains within SLO (baseline + 10%) during simulated transient upstream degradations
No user-facing increase in 5xx error rate during staged failover tests beyond incident baseline
Mechanism can be toggled per-service via feature flag and configured with region-specific parameters
Docs updated: operator playbook and runbook entries added to Console > Failover > Health gating
rollout_plan: 1) Feature flag behind service-level toggle. 2) Canary: enable on 5% of instances in staging region and run chaos tests for 48h. 3) Gradual rollout to non-critical production regions (10% -> 50% -> 100%) while monitoring autoscaler cycles and SLOs. 4) Full rollout to primary failover regions after two successful production canaries. 5) Post-rollout retrospective and permanent runbook update.
testing_plan: Unit tests for health token lifecycle and gating logic
Integration test: synthetic KV latency spikes with health token hold for configured window
Load test: 30m failover simulation with realistic traffic replay from last outage (use archived trace: traces/2026-02-14-failover-replay)
Chaos test: ECS node termination during tokenized readiness window to ensure no N+X loss of capacity
Canary metrics: autoscaler_event_rate, replica_count, cache_warm_miss_rate, p99_latency, p50_latency, 5xx_rate
metrics: replica_churn_count (scale up + scale down) per 30m window
implementation_notes: Introduce lightweight token store per instance (in-memory with optional persistence) to record recent health failures and hold readiness for token TTL
Health signals to aggregate: model runtime error rate, kv-cache-miss ratio, kernel OOMs, grpc upstream timeouts
Readiness evaluation now requires: healthy probes AND token_count == 0 OR token_age > configured_release_window
Staggered release: when multiple instances recover simultaneously, add jittered release offsets to avoid thundering-herd on cache rehydration
Autoscaler integration: expose derived stable_ready_count metric; autoscaler uses stable_ready_count rather than raw_ready_count for scaling decisions (configurable fallback)
Add feature flag in config-service: health_gating.v1 with per-service parameters: token_ttl_ms, release_jitter_ms, use_stable_ready_count
risks: If token TTL is too long we risk under-provisioning during genuine recoveries — could increase latency
Incorrect aggregation of signals could mask real failures and delay healing; need careful signal selection and thresholds
Edge-case: cascading termination during token hold could reduce net capacity; must ensure autoscaler uses fallback when total capacity drops below safety threshold
Operational complexity: new metric (stable_ready_count) must be reliable and instrumented across regions before rollout
outage_mitigation: Rollback via feature flag. Pre-configure autoscaler emergency override policy: if observed serving capacity falls below 85% of desired for N=3 windows, ignore stable_ready_count and revert to raw_ready_count until operator intervention.
